name: may
workload: Single-thread hello-world HTTP server, wrk -d10 -t1 -c200, may_minihttp (stackful coroutines on may) vs tokio_minihttp
claimed_speedup: ~15% higher requests/sec than tokio_minihttp (116,181.73 req/s vs 100,650.94 req/s)
stars_or_usage: 2.4k stars; may_minihttp cited as "one of the fastest web frameworks" on the TechEmpower Framework Benchmark
tradeoffs: Stackful coroutines (via generator crate) instead of Rust's native async/await; blocking-style API; must avoid calling thread-blocking syscalls directly and be careful with thread-local storage across coroutine yields.
caveats: First-party wrk benchmark, single thread only, no CPU model or compiler flags stated; may/may_minihttp dual-licensed Apache-2.0 OR MIT.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:coroutine io_uring / topic:async-runtime; opened Xudong-Huang/may and Xudong-Huang/may_minihttp READMEs

name: Rain
workload: TCP echo server, wrk -t4 -c256 -d15s, both sides built in Release mode
claimed_speedup: ~12.6% higher requests/sec than Tokio (247,283 req/s vs 219,543 req/s)
compiler_and_flags: Release build; exact compiler/version not stated
tradeoffs: Per-core shared-nothing design with no work-stealing; relies on SO_REUSEPORT for kernel-level load balancing across cores instead of an application-level scheduler; Linux-only (epoll, eventfd, signalfd).
caveats: First-party benchmark; hardware stated but compiler/version not; single workload (TCP echo) only.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than tokio" -> wzxzhuxi/Rain README_EN.md

name: nexus-async-rt / nexus-async-web
workload: WebSocket send/recv over TLS loopback, 40B and 128B messages, rdtscp cycle-accurate + wall-clock throughput, CPU-pinned to separate physical cores
claimed_speedup: 3-5x faster than tokio-tungstenite on TLS loopback (54 ns/msg vs 177 ns/msg at 40B; 134 ns/msg vs 280 ns/msg at 128B)
hardware: Intel Core Ultra 7 165U (hybrid P+E cores), 2.69GHz base clock, Linux 6.18, taskset-pinned to physical P-cores, turbo on
tradeoffs: Ships two mutually-exclusive runtime backends (tokio-rt and its own nexus-async-rt); comparison is of a WebSocket/REST protocol layer, not a general-purpose reactor.
caveats: Most of the win is protocol/codec efficiency vs the tokio-tungstenite library, not the raw event loop: the same code running on nexus-async-rt vs plain Tokio is close to parity (64 vs 64 cycles p50 latency). No exact compiler version stated.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than tokio" -> Abso1ut3Zer0/nexus README

name: Courierust
workload: WebSocket codec encode/decode and loopback-TCP echo round trips at 64B-256KiB payloads, CI-verified via cargo bench --release
claimed_speedup: Echo loop 64B: 26.5 us/msg vs 37.2 us/msg for tokio-tungstenite (~29% faster); codec: 2.3-2.6x faster masked encode at small frames, ~10x faster masked encode at 256KiB
hardware: Windows; exact CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 5 stars; benchmark suite runs in CI on every PR/push
tradeoffs: One row (UTF-8 validation of streamed text) is ~1.9x slower than std::str::from_utf8, reported honestly.
caveats: Licensed under PolyForm Perimeter 1.0.1, a source-available but non-OSI license (code may be studied, not freely reused/redistributed). No CPU model given; authors note large-payload numbers vary 3-10x across repeated runs on shared hardware.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "outperforms tokio" -> blueokanna/Courierust benches/WS_BENCHMARK.md

name: uringcore
workload: Python asyncio drop-in replacement using io_uring: single-task latency (sleep(0), lock_acquire, future result) and gather(100) concurrency, syscall counts via strace
claimed_speedup: 2.9-3.3x faster single-task latency than uvloop (e.g. sleep(0): 4.26us vs 12.53us); 26x fewer syscalls than uvloop under gather(100)
tradeoffs: Requires Linux kernel 5.11+ (5.19+ for best features); SQPOLL mode needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN or 5.12+ unprivileged SQPOLL.
caveats: No CPU model or kernel version stated for the latency numbers; loses to uvloop on raw gather(100) latency itself (139us vs uvloop's 105us) despite far fewer syscalls; self-reported, dated Jan 2026.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:io-uring / io_uring event loop -> ankitkpandey1/uringcore README

name: Boost.Corosio
workload: Handler dispatch, socket throughput/latency, HTTP server, and timer benchmarks on Windows using the IOCP backend, 3 seconds per benchmark
claimed_speedup: 9-50% faster handler dispatch than Asio coroutines (e.g. concurrent post/run: 2.35 Mops/s vs 1.61 Mops/s, +46%); best multithreaded scaling (89% efficiency at 8 threads vs 58% for Asio coroutines and 53% for Asio callbacks); loses to Asio callbacks on single-threaded dispatch (-51%) and large-buffer bidirectional throughput (-2.6x)
hardware: Windows (IOCP backend); exact CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 84 stars; maintained by the Cpp Alliance (Boost.Asio's own maintainers)
tradeoffs: Socket I/O, latency and HTTP-server throughput are roughly equivalent to Asio; Asio still wins decisively on timer schedule/cancel throughput (10x) and large-buffer bidirectional socket throughput.
caveats: Unusually candid report that documents losses as well as wins; no CPU model or compiler/flags stated, so capped at tier C despite thorough methodology; Windows/IOCP only in this report.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than asio" -> cppalliance/corosio benchmark-report.adoc

name: see (see::sync)
workload: Watch-channel notify/borrow latency at 1, 4, 16, and 64 subscribers, single-threaded, sync variant
claimed_speedup: Up to 2.3x faster than tokio::sync::watch at 1 subscriber (84.9us vs 213.8us) and 11-23% faster at 4 and 64 subscribers; tokio is faster at 16 subscribers (1.14ms vs 1.52ms)
tradeoffs: Runtime-agnostic (works with tokio, smol, compio) but the unsync variant sacrifices thread-safety (Rc/RefCell/Cell) for speed; sync variant uses parking_lot::RwLock and is ~4-8x slower than unsync in single-threaded use.
caveats: Result is not uniformly a win (tokio wins at 16 subscribers) and this is reported honestly; no compiler/flags stated; measures a sync primitive, not a full reactor/event loop.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "outperforms tokio" -> compio-rs/see README

name: zokio
workload: Microbenchmarks of async_fn creation, await execution, task scheduling, memory allocation and I/O ops/sec, compared against stated approximate Tokio baseline figures
claimed_speedup: Claims 32x-96x faster than Tokio across microbenchmarks (e.g. task scheduling 145M ops/s vs ~1.5M ops/s; async_fn creation 3.2B ops/s vs ~100M ops/s)
tradeoffs: Compile-time-heavy Zig async design; extremely low adoption (5 stars) for the scale of claims made.
caveats: Tokio baseline numbers are given as approximate ("~100M ops/sec", "~50M ops/sec") rather than measured on the same hardware/run as the Zokio numbers; ratios of 32x-96x for what should be comparable primitive operations are implausible and likely compare non-equivalent workloads. Capped at tier C per the >50x implausibility rule; treat with strong skepticism.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than tokio" -> louloulin/zokio docs/en/performance.md

name: exec-rs
workload: Single-threaded TCP echo server at 50/200/500 connections and 4KB payload (P2300 std::execution sender/receiver design, exec_echo example) vs a tokio_echo baseline example
claimed_speedup: 10-26% higher req/s than Tokio across concurrency levels (e.g. 135,157 req/s vs 107,333 req/s at 500 connections "heavy" load)
tradeoffs: Implements the C++ P2300 std::execution proposal's sender/receiver model in Rust; several features (nested when_all, some sequence senders) are incomplete.
caveats: README claims Apache-2.0 but the repository has no LICENSE file and GitHub's API reports no detected license -- treat as unclear/reference until a LICENSE file is added. No hardware or compiler details stated for the benchmark.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "outperforms tokio" -> npuichigo/exec-rs README
